title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

reading.body:
This is a case of a model asserting fabricated information as fact, specifically a legal AI tool generating nonexistent case citations, false case titles, and invented quotations that were then submitted to a court in actual legal filings. The failure happened at the output stage of a professional workflow, where an attorney used an AI tool to support legal research and incorporated its results into court documents without verifying that the cited cases existed. Seven fabricated citations appeared across eight filings before the error was admitted.

The failure would have been caught by a straightforward verification step, checking each citation against an authoritative legal database before filing. No such check was performed, or if it was, it did not catch the fabrications. The attorneys subsequently admitted the error, apologized to the court and opposing party, and stated that their firm updated its AI policies, but the corrective steps came after the false filings had already been submitted.

What is not established is whether the AI tool itself was defective beyond normal known hallucination behavior, whether any court sanction resulted, or whether the fabricated citations materially affected any ruling in the case.

reports.title: State Farm defense lawyers admit AI generated fake cases in LA lawsuit
AI hallucinated case law in insurance company’s filings in L.A. County house fire dispute
AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

summary:
# Summary

State Farm's legal team apologized for filing court motions containing fabricated legal cases, citations, and quotes in a lawsuit brought by Los Angeles homeowner Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga. The plaintiff sued State Farm and others after a 2020 fire left her home uninhabitable, and subsequent water damage and approval delays prevented repairs from being completed. She and her husband exhausted their savings, declared bankruptcy, and lost their home to foreclosure. State Farm lawyer Jacquelene Robinson admitted using an AI tool called Irys that incorrectly generated seven nonexistent case citations across eight filings, along with false case titles and quotes.

Lead counsel Kenneth Katel apologized to the court and plaintiff, accepting responsibility for the filings and stating his firm updated its AI policies. The case is scheduled for trial in October. This incident reflects a broader trend, with 41 percent of law firms now using generative AI. A Paris-based database has identified nearly 1,900 legal hallucination cases worldwide, mostly in the United States, prompting increased scrutiny of AI use in the legal profession.
